content: Boutonneuse fever, also known as Kenya tick typhus, Marseilles fever, or Mediterranean spotted fever, is a febrile illness caused by the bacterium Rickettsia conorii. This bacterium is transmitted to humans through the bite of the dog tick, Rhipicephalus sanguineus. The disease is endemic in regions surrounding the Mediterranean Sea. The incubation period for Boutonneuse fever is approximately seven days. Patients typically present with symptoms such as fever, chills, muscle pain (myalgias), joint pain (arthralgias), headache, and sensitivity to light (photophobia). On physical examination, a characteristic black eschar, known as tache noire, may be observed at the site of the tick bite. Around the fourth day of illness, a rash (exanthem) often develops, which initially appears as macular lesions and may progress to maculopapular or petechial forms. The diagnosis of Boutonneuse fever is confirmed through serologic testing. Common diagnostic methods include the Weil-Felix test, which detects agglutination of Proteus OX strains, as well as more specific assays such as enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) or immunofluorescence assays. Treatment for Boutonneuse fever primarily involves antimicrobial therapy. For adults, the preferred regimen is doxycycline, administered as 200 mg orally twice daily for one day, or alternatively, 200 mg or 100 mg orally twice daily for two to five days. In cases where doxycycline is contraindicated, alternative regimens include josamycin (1 g every eight hours for seven days) or ciprofloxacin. For children weighing less than 100 pounds, the preferred treatment is doxycycline at a dose of 2.2 mg/kg orally twice daily. For children weighing more than 100 pounds, the regimen mirrors that of adults, with 200 mg orally twice daily for one day, followed by 200 mg twice daily or 100 mg twice daily for two to five days. In children under eight years of age, alternative regimens include josamycin (2.2 mg/kg every 12 hours for five days) or clarithromycin (15 mg/kg in two divided doses daily for seven days) combined with azithromycin (10 mg/kg once daily for three days). Boutonneuse fever shares similarities with other rickettsial diseases, such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever, and should be considered in the differential diagnosis of febrile illnesses in endemic areas.
